screens.title: Track A: Mobile Inverted Pendulum Simulation
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will build a complete understanding of the Mobile Inverted Pendulum, a two-wheeled robot that balances a chassis like a broomstick on your hand. We start by modeling the dynamics using Lagrangian mechanics so you can see why the equations are nonlinear and coupled between wheel motion and pendulum angle. Then we linearize the model around the upright equilibrium, write a state-space form, and design cascade PD loops: a fast inner balance loop for angle and a slower outer loop for position. You will also implement an Extended Kalman Filter to fuse noisy IMU and encoder data and run a MATLAB simulation with ode45 to observe position and angle over time. Practically, this chapter ties dynamics, control, estimation, and simulation into one capstone exercise that mirrors real balancing systems like personal transporters. By the end you will understand the limits of linear controllers, how to tune PD gains, and why an EKF improves state estimates. Consider: what happens when you ask a balancing robot to move quickly while maintaining stability?

screens.title: MIP states and sensors
screens.narratorSegment: First, we clarify what a Mobile Inverted Pendulum carries as state and what sensors tell us. The canonical state vector for the MIP is four-dimensional: wheel position x, wheel velocity x-dot, pendulum angle theta, and pendulum angular velocity theta-dot. Wheel encoders provide odometry giving wheel rotation and typically allow a measured x-dot; the IMU gives an accelerometer and gyroscope, which after filtering provide angle and angular velocity measurements for theta and theta-dot. Concretely, your EKF will treat measurements as a vector z containing theta from the IMU, theta-dot from gyro, and x-dot from encoders. A common misconception is assuming you can read all states directly; in practice, sensors are noisy and partial, so you must fuse them to estimate unmeasured states and reduce noise. For example, an encoder might drift during slip, and the IMU angle estimate may be biased under vibration. The takeaway is to model which states are observed, which are inferred, and to make conservative assumptions about sensor noise when you design the EKF and controller. How will you keep the controller robust when a sensor temporarily degrades?

keyIdea.title: State & measurements
keyIdea.text: x, ẋ, θ, θ̇ are the core states; IMU and encoders provide noisy, partial measurements to be fused by estimation.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › MIP states and sensors
State vector
  • x — wheel position
  • ẋ — wheel velocity
  • θ — pendulum angle (rad)
  • θ̇ — pendulum angular velocity
Example

A typical measurement vector is [θ_imu; θ̇_imu; ẋ_encoder]. Use these to feed the EKF update step.

Sensors and limitations
  • IMU: noisy angle and gyro bias under vibration.
  • Encoders: good for relative motion but can slip or drift.
  • EKF: treats sensor noise explicitly via R and process noise Q.
Common mistake

Assuming encoder-derived velocity is noise-free. Always model measurement uncertainty and include it in R.

Concrete example

If θ is 0.1 rad and ẋ is 0.2 m/s, EKF prediction and an IMU update will correct biases and reduce variance.

Why it matters

Accurate state estimates let the balance controller use precise angle error and angular velocity feedback, which are time-critical.

Key takeaway

Treat sensors as partial and noisy; plan estimation accordingly so the controller receives reliable state information.

screens.title: Nonlinear Lagrangian dynamics
screens.narratorSegment: The MIP dynamics arise from Lagrangian mechanics and produce coupled, nonlinear differential equations. At a high level, the wheel-base mass and pendulum mass interact: wheel accelerations influence pendulum accelerations through products with cos and sin of the pendulum angle, and the pendulum's angular velocity contributes centrifugal terms. The source equations show two nonlinear relationships: one that links (M + m) times the wheel acceleration plus coupling terms to the applied force, and another that relates pendulum angular acceleration with gravity and wheel acceleration. A concrete example: when the pendulum leans forward, a forward motor torque produces both forward acceleration and a reaction that changes pendulum motion; the sin and cos terms make this coupling angle-dependent. A common misconception is to drop nonlinear terms too early; for large tilts the linear approximation breaks and control will likely fail. The practical takeaway is to implement the full nonlinear dynamics function for simulation, but use linearization only for controller design around theta equals zero. When you test in MATLAB, simulate both the nonlinear model and the linear controller to observe the valid operating region.

keyIdea.text: Use the full Lagrangian equations in simulation, and remember sin and cos terms create angle-dependent coupling between wheels and pendulum.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Nonlinear dynamics
Key equations (verbal)
  • Wheel equation: inertia plus pendulum coupling equals applied force.
  • Pendulum equation: inertia and gravity balance acceleration coupling and applied torque effects.
  • Nonlinear terms: sin(θ), cos(θ), and θ̇² create angle-dependent behaviors.
Concrete scenario

A sudden forward torque when θ is positive produces larger forward acceleration than at small θ because cos(θ) scales the coupling terms.

Simulation advice
  • Implement the full nonlinear function for ode45 to observe realistic behavior.
  • Use small time steps and check for energy growth that signals numerical issues.
  • Keep initial tilt small when testing linear controllers.
Misconception

Treating θ̇² as negligible for all conditions. It can dominate at large rotation rates and change stability.

Why this matters

Nonlinear simulation reveals the true recovery region and helps you choose safe initial conditions and gain ranges.

Example implementation

Code the two differential equations directly in your dynamics function for ode45 and test different initial angles.

Key takeaway

Use the nonlinear model for simulation fidelity; reserve linear models for controller synthesis around small angles.

screens.title: Linearization around the upright equilibrium
screens.narratorSegment: Linearization simplifies the nonlinear MIP equations by expanding sine and cosine around the upright equilibrium where theta equals zero. Practically, this means sin(theta) becomes approximately theta and cos(theta) becomes approximately one, and the theta-dot squared term can be neglected near small angles. The linearized two-equation system yields simpler expressions where wheel acceleration and pendulum angular acceleration are linearly related to the applied force. From these linear relations you can assemble state-space matrices A and B for the state vector [x; ẋ; θ; θ̇]. A concrete example: substituting theta equals zero yields constant coefficients that depend on M, m, L, and I; these entries populate the A matrix and show how torque maps to accelerations. A common misconception is assuming linearization works far from equilibrium; it does not. If the initial tilt is large, the linear controller based on A and B may not stabilize the system. The practical lesson is to derive A and B symbolically or numerically, verify eigenvalues for stability under the open-loop system, and then design a controller that places closed-loop poles in desired locations. Linearization around the upright equilibrium means linearization is valid only near theta = 0; use it to compute a and b and design controllers, but always verify operating region with nonlinear simulation.. In practical terms, from nonlinear equations to state-space a and b matrices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Linearize wisely
keyIdea.text: Linearization is valid only near theta = 0; use it to compute A and B and design controllers, but always verify operating region with nonlinear simulation.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Linearization
Linearization steps
  1. Set θ = 0 and θ̇ = 0 at equilibrium.
  2. Approximate sin(θ) ≈ θ and cos(θ) ≈ 1 for small θ.
  3. Neglect θ̇² terms near equilibrium.
  4. Solve algebraically to write ẍ and θ̈ as linear functions of states and input F.
  5. Assemble A and B matrices for ẋ = A x + B u.
Misconception

Linearization guarantees local validity only. Always test the linear controller on the nonlinear model to confirm stability margins.

What A and B reveal
  • A shows how states influence derivatives; cross-terms indicate coupling between x and θ.
  • B shows how motor force affects accelerations based on system masses and geometry.
Key takeaway

Compute A and B to design state-feedback or LQR controls; then verify with nonlinear simulation to ensure the controller works under realistic conditions.

screens.title: Cascade PD control architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Cascade PD control splits the task into two nested loops: a fast inner loop that maintains pendulum upright and a slower outer loop that commands the robot's position. The inner loop controls angle using τ_balance equals Kp_theta times angle error plus Kd_theta times angular velocity error; it must act quickly because balance dynamics are fast. The outer loop computes a desired tilt from position error: x_des equals Kp_x times position error plus Kd_x times velocity error, then θ_des is x_des divided by L. This structure keeps the high-bandwidth balancing task isolated from slower position control. A concrete example: to move forward to x_target, the position loop commands a small forward tilt; the inner loop immediately acts to hold that tilt without oscillation. A common confusion is trying a single PD controller for both angle and position; it fails because gains that stabilize position may be too slow for balance, and gains tuned for balance may cause aggressive position oscillations. The takeaway: treat time scales separately and tune inner loop before outer loop, then test combined behavior on the nonlinear model.

keyIdea.title: Why cascade
keyIdea.text: Separate fast balance control from slower position control to simplify tuning and ensure stability across time scales.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Cascade PD
Inner loop — Balance

Control law: τ_balance = Kp_theta (θ_des − θ) + Kd_theta (0 − θ̇). Designed for speed and damping to keep θ near zero despite disturbances.

Tuning tip: prioritize damping to avoid high-frequency oscillation; increase derivative gain carefully to avoid noise amplification.
Outer loop — Position

Compute x_des = Kp_x (x_target − x) + Kd_x (0 − ẋ). Convert to θ_des = x_des / L to command the inner loop. Designed with lower bandwidth than inner loop.

Tuning tip: adjust position gains so θ_des remains small and within linearization limits.
Concrete example

At t=3s set x_target=2m; outer loop commands small θ_des, inner loop moves wheels to track θ_des until the robot reaches the target.

Common mistake

Tuning both loops simultaneously without locking inner loop first. Always tune inner balance to be fast and stable first.

Key takeaway

Nested loops simplify design: inner loop keeps angle small, outer loop moves position by commanding small tilts.

screens.title: PD controller implementation
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing the PD controller is straightforward once you separate the loops. The inner loop computes torque based on angle error and angular velocity; the outer loop computes a desired tilt from position error and velocity and scales it by the pendulum length. In practice you compute x_des from position error, then θ_des = x_des / L, and feed that into the inner PD. Concrete example: with Kp_theta equal to fifty and Kd_theta equal to ten the inner loop responds strongly to small angle errors. A common misconception is to make Kp_theta excessively large to eliminate steady-state error; this can excite high-frequency oscillations due to sensor noise and actuator limits. When coding, keep anti-windup and saturation in mind for the motor torque, and test with different initial tilts to observe performance. The takeaway is to implement both loops in your dynamics function so the applied force F returned to the integrator reflects the nested control law, and then instrument the simulation to plot angle and position over time for tuning. PD controller implementation means compute x_des from position pd, map to θ_des = x_des/l, then compute f using angle pd with saturation and safety limits.. In practical terms, compute torque from angle and position errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: PD coding
keyIdea.text: Compute x_des from position PD, map to θ_des = x_des/L, then compute F using angle PD with saturation and safety limits.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › PD Controller
Controller logic (verbal)
  1. Compute position error and x_des with Kp_x and Kd_x.
  2. Compute θ_des = x_des / L.
  3. Compute torque F = Kp_theta (θ_des − θ) + Kd_theta (0 − θ̇).
  4. Saturate F to motor limits and send to dynamics.
Pro tip

Tune the inner loop first. Log θ and θ̇ to confirm inner-loop bandwidth before tuning outer loop gains.

Code example (MATLAB style)
% Compute outer loop desired tilt
x_error = x_target - x;
x_des = Kp_x * x_error + Kd_x * (0 - x_dot);
theta_des = x_des / L;

% Inner loop torque
F = Kp_theta * (theta_des - theta) + Kd_theta * (0 - theta_dot);
% Saturate
F = max(min(F, F_max), -F_max);
Concrete example

With Kp_theta=50 and Kd_theta=10 a small 0.1 rad tilt corrects quickly; observe if oscillation appears when Kp_theta is raised too far.

Common mistake

Applying large torque without saturation. Physical motors have limits; include saturations to avoid unrealistic simulations or damage in hardware.

Key takeaway

Implement nested PD logic directly in the dynamics so the integrator sees the closed-loop input at every time step.

screens.title: EKF structure and MATLAB update
screens.narratorSegment: The Extended Kalman Filter fuses nonlinear model predictions with linearized measurement updates. For the MIP, use the linearized A and B matrices for prediction in discrete time or apply continuous-time prediction approximations. The EKF routine consists of a prediction: x_pred equals A times x plus B times F, and P_pred equals A P A transpose plus Q. Then assemble the measurement matrix H that maps the state to measured quantities: typically theta, theta-dot, and x-dot. Compute the Kalman gain K, update the state with the innovation z minus H x_pred, and update covariance P. A concrete coding example in MATLAB uses the given script: compute x_pred, compute P_pred, build H, compute K, then x = x_pred + K (z - H * x_pred). A frequent misconception is to confuse a simple complementary filter with an EKF: EKF explicitly tracks covariance and corrects for correlated uncertainties and model errors. When tuning, if your R is too small, the EKF over-trusts noisy measurements and may produce choppy estimates; if Q is too large, the filter trusts the model too little. The practical takeaway is to instrument and plot P diagonal entries, estimated states, and measurement residuals to guide tuning.

keyIdea.title: EKF essentials
keyIdea.text: Use prediction with A and B, update with H and R, and tune Q and R while monitoring residuals and covariance growth.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › EKF
EKF steps (verbal)
  1. Predict: x_pred = A x + B F; P_pred = A P A' + Q.
  2. Build measurement matrix H for θ, θ̇, ẋ.
  3. Compute K = P_pred H' / (H P_pred H' + R).
  4. Update: x = x_pred + K (z − H x_pred); P = (I − K H) P_pred.
Misconception

Treating EKF as a black box. Inspect residuals and covariance to understand filter behavior and to tune Q and R properly.

MATLAB snippet
% EKF prediction and update
x_pred = A * x + B * F;
P_pred = A * P * A' + Q;

H = [0 0 1 0; 0 0 0 1; 0 1 0 0];
K = P_pred * H' / (H * P_pred * H' + R);

x = x_pred + K * (z - H * x_pred);
P = (eye(4) - K * H) * P_pred;
Concrete example

Add Gaussian noise to IMU and encoder signals and observe that the EKF estimate smooths angle and velocity traces while reflecting slow drifts in P.

Tuning reminder

Increase Q for model uncertainty, increase R for less trust in sensors. Watch innovation magnitudes to guide tuning.

Key takeaway

EKF requires careful tuning and diagnostics. Use plots of residuals and covariance to gain confidence in your estimates.

screens.title: MATLAB simulation with ode45

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › MATLAB simulation
Simulation recipe
  1. Write mip_dynamics(t,x,...) that returns x_dot using nonlinear equations and PD control.
  2. Set parameters and initial state x0 with small tilt, e.g., 0.1 rad.
  3. Call ode45(@(t,x) mip_dynamics(...), tspan, x0).
  4. Run EKF updates against simulated noisy measurements and log estimates.
  5. Plot position and angle subplots to inspect response.
MATLAB plotting example
% Simulate
tspan = [0 10];
x0 = [0; 0; 0.1; 0];
[t,x] = ode45(@(t,x) mip_dynamics(t,x,...), tspan, x0);

figure;
subplot(2,1,1); plot(t, x(:,1)); ylabel('Position (m)');
subplot(2,1,2); plot(t, x(:,3)); ylabel('Pendulum Angle (rad)'); xlabel('Time (s)');
Concrete test

At t=3s set x_target=2m and watch the angle tilt forward and then back to stop at the target.

Common mistake

Forgetting to add sensor noise; the EKF must be tested with realistic noise to tune Q and R properly.

Key takeaway

Use simulation to compare true state and EKF estimate and iterate on controller gains and filter covariances until behavior matches requirements.

screens.title: Stability limits and fail-safe mechanisms
screens.narratorSegment: The MIP is inherently unstable and the linear controller only works within a region of attraction around the upright equilibrium. Typically, beyond approximately thirty degrees the small-angle approximations break and the controller cannot recover. In simulation you can demonstrate this by initializing theta at a large value and observing the system fall. For physical systems, the safety strategy is to add fall detection and motor shutoff: if absolute theta exceeds a safety threshold or if the control output saturates persistently, disable motors to prevent damage. A concrete example: if theta crosses 0.5 radians in simulation, log a fail state and examine actuator commands prior to failure to see how the controller saturated. A common misconception is treating software recovery alone as sufficient; hardware limits and time delays can prevent recovery even if the controller would be correct in theory. The takeaway is to instrument both simulation and hardware with threshold checks, and to test fail-safe triggers under noisy sensor conditions to avoid false positives or missed detections. Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Stability & Safety
Stability region

Linear controllers are valid near θ = 0. Beyond a threshold angle, nonlinear terms dominate and recovery becomes unlikely. Test limits in simulation by increasing initial tilt until controller fails.

Instrument plots to show when torque saturates and when θ grows rapidly, indicating a fall.
Fail-safe design
  • Threshold check on |θ|, e.g., 30°–50° depending on system.
  • Motor shutoff and brake engage when threshold exceeded.
  • Log pre-fail sensor traces for debugging and tuning.
Misconception

Assuming the controller will always recover if you increase gains. In hardware, actuator limits, delays, and sensor noise can prevent recovery regardless of gains.

Concrete example

Simulate with initial θ = 1 rad and plot torque saturation and angle growth to demonstrate failure modes.

Why it matters

Fail-safes prevent hardware damage and provide useful logs for tuning and debugging after a fall.

Key takeaway

Always pair controllers with safety monitoring and actuator limits; test fail-safe triggers in simulation under noise before hardware trials.

screens.title: Tuning experiments and expected behaviors
screens.narratorSegment: When you run tuning experiments you will see characteristic responses depending on PD gains and EKF tuning. With too-low Kp_theta the inner loop is weak and the pendulum will drift and eventually fall, showing large angle deviations in the plot. With too-high Kp_theta you may get high-frequency oscillations that appear as noisy rapid angle corrections; this often indicates excessive gain or derivative action amplifying sensor noise. A well-tuned inner loop yields quick damping of small tilts while the outer loop causes smooth small tilts to track position commands. For the EKF, an R matrix that is too small makes the filter follow noisy measurements too closely, producing choppy estimates; an overly large Q makes the filter slow to respond. A concrete scenario: set Kp_theta low and observe divergence, then gradually increase Kp_theta until the angle response is critically damped and stable. A useful closing question is: how do you balance responsiveness against noise amplification when choosing derivative gains and measurement covariances? Tuning experiments and expected behaviors means under-tuned inner loops lead to falls; over-tuned loops create oscillation. ekf tuning balances noise rejection and responsiveness.. Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Tuning experiments
Gain scenarios
  • Too low Kp_theta: slow corrections, possible fall.
  • Too high Kp_theta: high-frequency oscillation and noise amplification.
  • Good tuning: quick, well-damped response and smooth position tracking.
EKF tuning effects
  • R too small: filter chases noise.
  • Q too large: filter slow to adapt.
  • Balanced: smooth estimates that track true state without oversensitivity.
Concrete exercise

Run three gain sets and plot angle traces. Explain why each trace behaves as it does.

Common mistake

Changing inner and outer gains together without isolating effects. Change one loop at a time to attribute effects properly.

Key takeaway

Systematic experiments and well-labeled plots make tuning decisions reproducible and justifiable in your report.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will build a complete understanding of the Mobile Inverted Pendulum, a two-wheeled robot that balances a chassis like a broomstick on your hand. We start by modeling the dynamics using Lagrangian mechanics so you can see why the equations are nonlinear and coupled between wheel motion and pendulum angle. Then we linearize the model around the upright equilibrium, write a state-space form, and design cascade PD loops: a fast inner balance loop for angle and a slower outer loop for position. You will also implement an Extended Kalman Filter to fuse noisy IMU and encoder data and run a MATLAB simulation with ode45 to observe position and angle over time. Practically, this chapter ties dynamics, control, estimation, and simulation into one capstone exercise that mirrors real balancing systems like personal transporters. By the end you will understand the limits of linear controllers, how to tune PD gains, and why an EKF improves state estimates. Consider: what happens when you ask a balancing robot to move quickly while maintaining stability?

By the end of this chapter you will model the mobile inverted pendulum dynamics, design cascade PD controllers, implement an Extended Kalman Filter, and run MATLAB simulations to validate stability. First, you will build a state model that includes wheel position and velocity and pendulum angle and angular velocity, forming a four-state vector. Then you will derive the nonlinear Lagrangian equations and see how sin and cos terms create coupling between translational and rotational dynamics. You will linearize around the upright equilibrium to produce a state-space representation suitable for controller design. Third, you will design nested PD loops: a fast inner loop that keeps the pendulum upright and a slower outer loop that commands position via a desired tilt. Fourth, you will implement an EKF that fuses IMU angle and gyro readings with wheel encoder velocity to estimate the full state under sensor noise. Each objective builds toward a working MATLAB simulation that demonstrates stability limits and fail-safe considerations.

These objectives map to concrete actions you will perform. You will write the nonlinear dynamics function used by MATLAB's integrator, validate linearization algebra around theta equals zero, and compute state-space matrices A and B for controller design. You will design PD gains and demonstrate the difference between too-low and too-high angle gains using time traces of angle and position. For the EKF you will implement prediction and update steps, tune process and measurement covariances, and plot estimated versus true states under added Gaussian noise. Finally, you will create plots of position and pendulum angle over a ten-second run, introduce a step position command at three seconds, and explain the robot's tilt behavior during acceleration and stopping. Each assessment item asks for plots and brief explanations showing why the chosen gains and covariances produce the observed behavior.

First, we clarify what a Mobile Inverted Pendulum carries as state and what sensors tell us. The canonical state vector for the MIP is four-dimensional: wheel position x, wheel velocity x-dot, pendulum angle theta, and pendulum angular velocity theta-dot. Wheel encoders provide odometry giving wheel rotation and typically allow a measured x-dot; the IMU gives an accelerometer and gyroscope, which after filtering provide angle and angular velocity measurements for theta and theta-dot. Concretely, your EKF will treat measurements as a vector z containing theta from the IMU, theta-dot from gyro, and x-dot from encoders. A common misconception is assuming you can read all states directly; in practice, sensors are noisy and partial, so you must fuse them to estimate unmeasured states and reduce noise. For example, an encoder might drift during slip, and the IMU angle estimate may be biased under vibration. The takeaway is to model which states are observed, which are inferred, and to make conservative assumptions about sensor noise when you design the EKF and controller. How will you keep the controller robust when a sensor temporarily degrades?

The MIP dynamics arise from Lagrangian mechanics and produce coupled, nonlinear differential equations. At a high level, the wheel-base mass and pendulum mass interact: wheel accelerations influence pendulum accelerations through products with cos and sin of the pendulum angle, and the pendulum's angular velocity contributes centrifugal terms. The source equations show two nonlinear relationships: one that links (M + m) times the wheel acceleration plus coupling terms to the applied force, and another that relates pendulum angular acceleration with gravity and wheel acceleration. A concrete example: when the pendulum leans forward, a forward motor torque produces both forward acceleration and a reaction that changes pendulum motion; the sin and cos terms make this coupling angle-dependent. A common misconception is to drop nonlinear terms too early; for large tilts the linear approximation breaks and control will likely fail. The practical takeaway is to implement the full nonlinear dynamics function for simulation, but use linearization only for controller design around theta equals zero. When you test in MATLAB, simulate both the nonlinear model and the linear controller to observe the valid operating region.

Linearization simplifies the nonlinear MIP equations by expanding sine and cosine around the upright equilibrium where theta equals zero. Practically, this means sin(theta) becomes approximately theta and cos(theta) becomes approximately one, and the theta-dot squared term can be neglected near small angles. The linearized two-equation system yields simpler expressions where wheel acceleration and pendulum angular acceleration are linearly related to the applied force. From these linear relations you can assemble state-space matrices A and B for the state vector [x; ẋ; θ; θ̇]. A concrete example: substituting theta equals zero yields constant coefficients that depend on M, m, L, and I; these entries populate the A matrix and show how torque maps to accelerations. A common misconception is assuming linearization works far from equilibrium; it does not. If the initial tilt is large, the linear controller based on A and B may not stabilize the system. The practical lesson is to derive A and B symbolically or numerically, verify eigenvalues for stability under the open-loop system, and then design a controller that places closed-loop poles in desired locations. Linearization around the upright equilibrium means linearization is valid only near theta = 0; use it to compute a and b and design controllers, but always verify operating region with nonlinear simulation.. In practical terms, from nonlinear equations to state-space a and b matrices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Cascade PD control splits the task into two nested loops: a fast inner loop that maintains pendulum upright and a slower outer loop that commands the robot's position. The inner loop controls angle using τ_balance equals Kp_theta times angle error plus Kd_theta times angular velocity error; it must act quickly because balance dynamics are fast. The outer loop computes a desired tilt from position error: x_des equals Kp_x times position error plus Kd_x times velocity error, then θ_des is x_des divided by L. This structure keeps the high-bandwidth balancing task isolated from slower position control. A concrete example: to move forward to x_target, the position loop commands a small forward tilt; the inner loop immediately acts to hold that tilt without oscillation. A common confusion is trying a single PD controller for both angle and position; it fails because gains that stabilize position may be too slow for balance, and gains tuned for balance may cause aggressive position oscillations. The takeaway: treat time scales separately and tune inner loop before outer loop, then test combined behavior on the nonlinear model.

Implementing the PD controller is straightforward once you separate the loops. The inner loop computes torque based on angle error and angular velocity; the outer loop computes a desired tilt from position error and velocity and scales it by the pendulum length. In practice you compute x_des from position error, then θ_des = x_des / L, and feed that into the inner PD. Concrete example: with Kp_theta equal to fifty and Kd_theta equal to ten the inner loop responds strongly to small angle errors. A common misconception is to make Kp_theta excessively large to eliminate steady-state error; this can excite high-frequency oscillations due to sensor noise and actuator limits. When coding, keep anti-windup and saturation in mind for the motor torque, and test with different initial tilts to observe performance. The takeaway is to implement both loops in your dynamics function so the applied force F returned to the integrator reflects the nested control law, and then instrument the simulation to plot angle and position over time for tuning. PD controller implementation means compute x_des from position pd, map to θ_des = x_des/l, then compute f using angle pd with saturation and safety limits.. In practical terms, compute torque from angle and position errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Extended Kalman Filter fuses nonlinear model predictions with linearized measurement updates. For the MIP, use the linearized A and B matrices for prediction in discrete time or apply continuous-time prediction approximations. The EKF routine consists of a prediction: x_pred equals A times x plus B times F, and P_pred equals A P A transpose plus Q. Then assemble the measurement matrix H that maps the state to measured quantities: typically theta, theta-dot, and x-dot. Compute the Kalman gain K, update the state with the innovation z minus H x_pred, and update covariance P. A concrete coding example in MATLAB uses the given script: compute x_pred, compute P_pred, build H, compute K, then x = x_pred + K (z - H * x_pred). A frequent misconception is to confuse a simple complementary filter with an EKF: EKF explicitly tracks covariance and corrects for correlated uncertainties and model errors. When tuning, if your R is too small, the EKF over-trusts noisy measurements and may produce choppy estimates; if Q is too large, the filter trusts the model too little. The practical takeaway is to instrument and plot P diagonal entries, estimated states, and measurement residuals to guide tuning.

Running a MATLAB simulation ties the model, control, and estimator together so you can observe closed-loop behavior. Implement a dynamics function that takes state and time and returns derivatives using the nonlinear Lagrangian equations and the PD control law. Use ode45 to integrate from zero to ten seconds with an initial small tilt, for example theta equals 0.1 rad. Log states at each step and run the EKF in discrete time synchronized with your integrator outputs or run the EKF inside the integrator callback when using small steps.
